content: The publication titled National Tuberculosis Prevalence Surveys: What Diagnostic Algorithms Should Be Used in Future? was released by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2023. It is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-007391-3 and 978-92-4-007392-0. The document is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing users to copy, redistribute, and adapt the work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The document was authored by Katherine Floyd and Irwin Law, with contributions from Philippe Glaziou and Charalambos Sismanidis, all of whom are part of the Tuberculosis Monitoring, Evaluation, and Strategic Information (TME) unit within WHO’s Global Tuberculosis Programme (GTB). Analytical work was conducted by Sian Floyd, Philippe Glaziou, and Irwin Law, with additional data provided by the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND). The publication benefited from reviews by numerous experts and organizations, including Helen Ayles, Razia Fatima, Eveline Klinkenberg, Petra Haas, Nazir Ismail, Ikushi Onozaki, Samuel Schumacher, Marina Tadolini, Sabira Tahseen, Edine Tiemersma, and Norio Yamada. WHO acknowledges their invaluable input and insights. The publication builds on discussions and findings from various meetings and workshops, including those of the WHO Global Task Force on TB Impact Measurement, held between 2016 and 2022. These meetings involved national TB prevalence survey teams from countries such as Myanmar, South Africa, and Viet Nam, as well as technical partners and experts from the TB Reduction through Expanded Antiretroviral Treatment and Screening (TREATS) study. The document also incorporates evidence from unpublished FIND data and updated guidance on national TB prevalence surveys. The introduction highlights the global targets set by the United Nations Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and WHO’s Stop TB Strategy (2006–2015) to reduce the burden of tuberculosis (TB). These targets included halting and reversing TB incidence by 2015, reducing TB prevalence by 50% compared to 1990 levels, and reducing TB mortality by 50% compared to 1990 levels. The WHO Global Task Force on TB Impact Measurement was established in 2006 to ensure robust and consensus-based assessments of progress toward these targets at global, regional, and national levels. At the Task Force’s second meeting in 2007, three strategic areas of work were identified: strengthening routine surveillance systems (disease notification and vital registration), conducting national TB prevalence surveys in 22 global focus countries (GFCs), and periodically reviewing methods used by WHO to estimate TB disease burden. WHO issued its first guidance on national TB prevalence surveys in 2008, which was updated in 2010 (the lime book). The ultimate goal is for all countries to reliably track their TB epidemics using national disease notification and vital registration systems. However, in 2007, many countries lacked high-quality vital registration systems, and progress in establishing such systems was limited between 2000 and 2012. National TB prevalence surveys were included as a priority because routine surveillance data often could not reliably estimate the true burden of TB due to underreporting and underdiagnosis, particularly in countries with large private healthcare sectors or significant barriers to accessing public healthcare. National TB prevalence surveys have two main objectives: (1) to provide a reliable, direct measurement of the burden of TB disease in the population, especially when routine surveillance data are insufficient, and (2) to assess trends in TB burden over time, including progress toward global targets and milestones. These surveys focus on bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB in adults. Repeat surveys are particularly useful for assessing trends and the impact of interventions to reduce TB burden. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted TB diagnosis and treatment services, leading to potential increases in TB prevalence. In countries with significant disruptions, repeat surveys conducted shortly after the pandemic may not reliably detect changes in TB prevalence. In such cases, direct and precise measurements of TB burden are prioritized over trend assessments. National population-based surveys of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB in adults provide an alternative approach to measuring TB burden in the absence of high-quality routine surveillance systems. National TB prevalence surveys also offer additional benefits, such as documenting healthcare-seeking behavior, assessing variations in underreporting or underdiagnosis by age and sex, and quantifying the extent of underreporting to national authorities. These findings can inform the development or improvement of TB case-finding, diagnostic, and treatment interventions. The WHO Task Force updated its overarching purpose in 2016 to focus on measuring progress toward new milestones and targets for reducing TB incidence, mortality, and patient costs, as outlined in WHO’s End TB Strategy (2016–2035) and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs, 2015–2030). National TB prevalence surveys remain relevant for assessing trends in TB burden and informing incidence estimates, particularly in countries with high TB burden. By the end of 2022, a large number of national TB prevalence surveys had been completed, with some countries planning repeat surveys in 2023 or 2024. These surveys provide critical data for understanding the distribution of TB cases by age and sex, assessing healthcare-seeking behavior, and identifying gaps in TB diagnosis and reporting.
